speechtext:
That is
exactly what my hon. friends will do anyway; I have to take my chance on that. I do not like to insinuate, but I think hon. gentlemen in that corner have found themselves in a somewhat difficult position with reference to their registered vote on this matter. One or two of them at all events felt the same as I did and did not support the government in foisting on this country private ownership of a central bank.
The hon. gentleman also said that their attitude might influence the government in connection with what they were going to do with the bank. The government could have passed that legislation without a single vote being registered from that corner of the house; they did not need my hon. friends' votes to register the popular opinion of this house as indicated by the government majority. I must defend the position I took last summer-and I took it wherever I spoke- that I did not understand the attitude of hon. gentlemen on this question, and I do not yet. I merely say that either I was wrong in registering my vote against the bill, or they must be wrong in the attitude they took.
We still stand, as the hon. member for North Waterloo has indicated, for public ownership and control of this central bank. We believe that is the agency through which we can properly regulate this institution. Hon. gentlemen will disagree, and they have a right, if they see fit, to do so on this particular matter. We feel sufficient control can be exercised over the operations of the private banks to give the people of this country with whom they have business a square deal. I am not even going to blame the private banks for the condition in which we find ourselves to-day. What is the trouble with the Canadian people to-day in common with those of every other country? We have had too much
credit. Neither the members of the government nor the banks can escape this responsibility. Both have been guilty. I have heard the statement-and it is an expression we can all understand-that we spent money like drunken sailors, both governments and banks. Every institution did the same thing until we reached the stage that my hon. friend has so ably depicted this afternoon. We now find ourselves in a very unfortunate position. Let me put my attitude very clearly. I am not going to say that I am opposed to nationalization of banking, but I want first to nationalize the central bank and see how far that control can go. I do not wonder my good friend in believing in what he was voting for last year is disappointed. He freely admits that; he says that there is every evidence of it. The evidence is growing that private control is going to dominate the actions of this institution, and that is exactly what we felt and feared would happen. But at the same time I for one am not in a position to say that nationalization of private banking will cure the situation. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Rhodes) put his finger on the spot when he said:	We are all human
and we are doing the very best we can, what in our judgment is in the best interest for ourselves and for the public whom we serve. I do not believe if we had had our banks nationalized to-day we would have been saved from going into the morass of debt in which we now find ourselves. I can understand a situation where we would abolish interest altogether, what my good friend McGeer calls usury. Then the incentive disappears; this would take money out of the position of being a commodity and we would use it merely as a medium of exchange. I can understand that situation, but to say you are going to permit the usury system to continue and to transfer it from a private corporation to a publicly owned one and thus cure the difficulty in which we find ourselves, is something with respect to which I have very grave doubts, because while different men will be in control they will be human beings just the same.
I do want to be definitely understood as going to the extent of having control exercised publicly, nationally, of the central bank. I will go with my hon. friends a long distance in the way of restraint and restriction upon the operation of private banks. Possibly I will go the whole distance of nationalizing them if it can be demonstrated that the first step is a success and that the second is also a success. It may be all right to transform overnight the whole financial and banking
Nationalization of Banks

institutions of the country from private to public ownership, but I would not care to take such drastic action without a little more consideration than we are giving the matter at the present time. That is the only difference between them and me. We want the central bank to be publicly owned and controlled; we want that step to be taken. I doubt if my hon. friends over there would go to the extent indicated by the resolution moved this afternoon, the complete nationalization of all the banking institutions. I do not believe any system is perfect; I agree with the minister when he says that as long as we have human mentality administering the business of this country, we shall have mistakes. I do not agree that either by private or by public bodies they are made with the intention of having a harmful effect upon the public generally. But mistakes are made, and the government will have the same mentality, whether there is public or private control. But I agree thoroughly with the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre that the parliament of Canada cannot escape responsibility for the policies which will govern. We have a right to control these institutions which get from parliament the right to do business. In that I am at one with my hon. friends. But I regret that I cannot be with them in their attitude of last session in supporting what I consider a privately owned institution.
I am not going into details as to the central bank itself; I simply content myself with making my position clear on the question immediately before us.

subtopic: PROPOSAL THAT CREDIT AND CURRENCY SHALL BE CONTROLLED AND ADMINISTERED BY GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not think I have ever ventured to speak in this house before on a question of finance. We have so many financial experts in this corner that perhaps it was not necessary; besides, it is a rather dangerous proceeding for a person like myself. I should not have risen on this occasion had it not been for a statement made by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Rhodes) to the effect that in 1929 we were in a world gone mad. That statement is not very strange in itself, but it is strange if the implication is that we are at the present time in a sane world. In 1929 we had gone mad to the extent that we thought we could all get rich by buying bonds from each other or from the numerous bond salesmen. Now we believe that we must remain poor and in fact suffer privation because we connot find enough money to distribute the commodities that we can produce in such abundance. If the Minister 
of Finance suggests that that is an indication of sanity, then we differ in our definition of sanity.
What is the purpose of the resolution? It is to nationalize the banking facilities of Canada. Why do we want to nationalize the banking facilities of Canada, or what does nationalizing them mean? It means the transfer of the banking facilities from private to social control. It means taking out of the hands of private owners an important factor in production, and vesting the ownership in the community or the state, whichever term you may care to use. Why should we wish to do that? Because we feel to-day-I think everyone, even the Minister of Finance, will admit it; the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) has admitted it

that private ownership of the means of production leads to their use for the benefit of the owners always, and not in the interests of the people of the country. All that we are suggesting is that we should transfer these instruments of production and distribution from private ownership and place them in the hands of the community in order that they may be used for social benefit. Is there anything wrong with that? There is no other possible way in which that end can be accomplished except by transfer of ownership.
There is one point on which I think I must differ from the mover of the resolution. He stated that the control of industry by finance prevented industry from fulfilling its purpose. I can see what the hon. member for Wetaski-win (Mr. Irvine) meant by that; he takes it that the purpose of industry is to carry on production, to produce commodities to meet social needs. But that is not in fact the purpose of industry under private ownership. Under private ownership the purpose of industry is to produce property rights for the owners of the means of production. To-day the control of industry and of finance is in the same hands. If we do not use the nationalization of finance as the means of socializing and nationalizing industry we have not accomplished anything by socializing finance.
What gives a bank its value? What gives the Bank of Montreal its value, what gives the Canadian Bank of Commerce or the Royal bank or any bank its value? The fact that the community uses its services; that is what gives it value. If the community ceased to use its services the value of the bank to its shareholders would disappear. It is the community, the social organization of society, that gives to every economic and financial and business organization its value. The

Nationalization oj Banks
moment that institution is transferred into the hands of the community it is of no further value to the interests that formerly owned it, except in so far as they are part of the community; then they obtain value from it only in equal measure with the rest of the community. That is the primary reason why we seek to socialize not only our banking facilities but all our industrial processes as well; for if the community gives the value then the community should own and control and appropriate that value. That is impossible as long as we maintain the present basis of private ownership.
Now may I say a few words in regard to the action of some of us in this corner in voting for the Bank of Canada bill last year. The hon. member for West Edmonton (Mr. Stewart) tried very hard to justify his position, but it was not very convincing to me. The Liberal party, or at least a section of the Liberal party-and I am not sure but that it is only a section that is now advocating national control and ownership of the central bank-had been advocating that for quite a number of years before they came into office. At the Liberal convention of the western provinces, held in Winnipeg in 1917, a resolution was passed unanimously which read as follows:
That, in the opinion of this convention, the time has arrived for the reorganization of the barking system of Canada, so as to bring it more nearly within the democratic spirit of proper regulation and control by the people, and with this object in view, be it resolved

This is what they resolved:
1. The banking system of Canada should be placed under the control and regulation of a banking commission invested with plenary powers in all matters pertaining to banking, currency, coinage and credits, and, in particular, to regulate and control:
(a)	the issues of public currency;
(b)	the coinage of gold and silver;
And so on. That was in 1917. They came into office in 1922 and remained in office until 1930, but not one step was taken to make this policy operative. Furthermore the bank charters came up for revision in 1922. My friends in this corner who were here at that time tried to get the government of that day to put some of these policies into effect. I believe the hon. member for West Edmonton was a member of the government at that time. These are some of the things they were to regulate and control:
(a)	The issues of .public currency.
(b)	The coinage of gold and silver.
(c)	The purchase of bullion produced in Canada.
(d)	The amount of call money loaned outside of Canada.
(e)	Interlocking directorates.
(f)	The supervision of credits.
(g)	The capitalization of banks.
(h)	The payment of dividends.
(i)	The relations of subsidiary trust and money lending concerns to banks.
(j)	And generally, all such matters that are necessarily incident to the proper regulation and control of banking and currency.
I believe the present government have put paragraph (c) into effect. All those other financial activities ran rampant while hon. gentlemen to my right were in office, but not a line was put on the statute books to regulate or control any part of the system.

I must say that it makes me laugh every time I hear in this house of the dangers of political interference in connection with the central bank. Our bankers raise their hands in holy horror of government ownership and control, for fear of political interference. What do they mean? They just fear that someone else may get a finger In the pie instead of themselves; that is all. They are only afraid that someone else will get a hearing; they have had all the breaks so far, and they are afraid that someone else may get ahead of them. Shortly before I came east I was talking with one of the new members of the provincial legislature of British Columbia. He said the mine owners had a lobby and the lumber operators had a lobby. Everyone a person could imagine had a lobby-except the workers and farmers. They did not have lobbies. Of course the bankers have their lobbies and that is the reason they are opposed to political control, to government ownership.

Mr. Speaker, the remarks of the hon. member for West Edmonton (Mr. Stewart) have led me to believe that the Liberal leopard has not changed its spots, but that in the future it will continue to win its way back into power by stealth, rather than by coming out in the open. They called it the great betrayal. The hon. member for West Edmonton on many occasions, according to his own word's, referred to the so-called great betrayal of the group sitting in this corner.
So far as I know the leader of the party to which the hon. member for West Edmonton belongs has on no occasion, either in this house or out of it, stated that he was in favour of the nationalization of the banks, or even the nationalization of the central bank. It does not make any difference what the hon. member for West Edmonton or any other member in his party has to say, until we definitely know what the right hon. leader of the opposition has to say about this matter of banking; otherwise whatever the hon. member for West Edmonton has to say will be as sounding brass and tinkling cymbal; for the policy of the leader is the policy of the party. On no occasion have I heard of any alternative policy being offered by the official opposition either in this house or outside of it.
In all his speeches the hon. member for West Edmonton states, "If we get back into power, through the instrumentality of low tariffs, restoring old markets and finding new ones, we will bring back prosperity." And the exuberance, the extraordinary optimism, the extravagant hopefulness he has shown, and that shown by other hon. members behind him, would almost lead one to believe that when the official opposition got into power strawberries would grow on stinkweed, grain on sow thistles, bananas on poplar trees and other luscious fruits on a lot of other obnoxious plants which spread so profusely in western Canada. Such is the dream, but what is the reality? But never mind, O Canadian 92582-304
people; for the wizard leader of the opposition will lull you into sweet and opiate forgetfulness through the policy that the hon. member for West Edmonton has so eloquently promulgated throughout the length and breadth of the land. And when the autocratic Hitler sees the democratic King emerge from the valley wielding the big club of negotiation, fear will seize the great German nation and the hills and the valleys which were made to produce golden grain will go back to producing hops and grapes as before; and the bread that was made to feed German mouths will henceforth be made out of good Canadian wheat. And when 11 Duce hears of the recent provincial victories as well as the federal one he will have a fit of panic before this new international cave man, and shiploads of wheat will wend their way to the land of macaroni and spaghetti as hitherto. And the economically planned United States, seeing the condition of affairs in laissez-faire Canada, when the official opposition gets into power will send aeroplanes into the air which will throw bombs to destroy the artificial barriers existing between Canada and the United States. The French republic, with equal consternation, leaving well enough alone, will employ her farmers in the production oif perfumes, cosmetics, bric-a-brac and other delicatessen instead of letting them produce grain. That is the impression they intended to create throughout the west, and that is the impression the hon. member for West Edmonton has often tried to create right here in this house. There is no question about that.
So far as the resolution moved by the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Mackenzie) is concerned there can be no doubt about its alphabetic stupidity. It was no doubt drafted with the feeling that it might be heaven, hell or purgatory that his party would share, so he thought it very well to make friends everywhere. I did not intend to speak on this motion, but it would seem that to-day we appear to be running in a circle. One hon. member will get up and say, "Well, I would not have spoken had it not been for the hon. member who preceded me." I am afraid I am in the same position as three or four other hon. members who have just spoken about this banking question.
Yes, I was one who voted for the central bank last year, and I do not care whether a hundred members for West Edmonton go into the Vegreville constituency to decry the facts; I am quite prepared to tell the people in Vegreville why I voted, how I voted and

where I voted. There is no doubt that the ventral bank can foe made nationally owned at any- time, and if the official opposition gets into power, as the seer, the dean and the patriarch of the house, the member for Labelle (Mr. Bourassa) predicted only a few days ago, and if they are serious about making the central bank a national bank, I shall be prepared to give them not only one vote but, if I had them, one hundred votes.
Mr. JEAN-FRANCOIS POULIOT (Temis-oouata): Mr. Speaker, I have just listened to the speech of the hon. member for Vegre-ville (Mr. Luchkovich). He has not answered the question I put to the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation two years ago, namely in February, 1933, concerning the nationalization of the banks. If you, sir, would kindly allow me to adjourn this debate until eight o'clock I would have sufficient time to get Hansard of 1933 and read those questions to the members in the corner of the house, and in that way we would learn whether or not they are ready to answer them.
This is no time to make jokes about macaroni, spaghetti, sausages, delicatessen and so on. If the hon. member's stomach is empty, then he may go to dinner and have sausages, macaroni, spaghetti, tripe, gravy and anything like that. Let him eat pork, beef, or what he will; but that is no argument upon which to exercise one's brains. I expected some thought to come from so genial an hon. gentleman, but what did we have? We had a most indigestible menu, something that one could not eat, even with H.P. sauce. He recites the bill of fare in the midst of a dignified discussion of one of the most important problems of the day. We have these gentlemen with us who say: Let us nationalize the banks, nationalize the deposits which have been entrusted to the banks by the people of this country. Sir this is a matter of great concern to everyone who has a dollar in the banks. Would it be any better if the state owned and controlled all the money which has been deposited in the chartered banks of this country? That is the question, and it is one of momentous importance. It has already been discussed in this house, and discussed throughout the country. Not later than last fall there was a by-election in the city of Toronto, and a gentleman whom I know well was a candidate of the group who sit in the extreme left comer of this house. What was the result when the matter was submitted to the intelligent people of Toronto? It was this: the man who was the candidate of that group

or party to my left, call them what you like, got a minority vote, but his minority vote helped to elect the Tory candidate.
There is one difference only between the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) and the leader of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation group (Mr. Woodsworth); one is clean-shaven and the other is not. That is the only difference between the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) and the hon. member for West Calgary (Mr. Bennett). Two years ago in the month of February I asked fifty-five questions of the hon. gentleman who sits to my left, and I got no reply from any of them. They were all dumb-just as dumb as if they were ministers of the crown. No answer; and now the only answer we get, after two years in which they have had time enough to think over the matter, is jokes like those we have just heard or invective against one or other of the parties in this house. They cannot answer the questions that I asked, questions which were based on their program; and instead we hear jokes. It is all right, sir, to promise the moon. It is all right to say that someone will go up into the sky-the sky is the limit-and bring down the stars and offer them to the hon. member for Vegreville, but I say to the hon. member for Vegreville: while he may be a star, he is not a star from heaven, judging by the materialistic speech which I have just heard him deliver. It proved quite otherwise.
Do you believe, Mr. Speaker, that the widow with all her savings in the bank would agree to the nationalization of the banks, would agree to having her all which she has put in the bank controlled by such a gentleman as the hon. member for Vegreville, or by such an economist as the hon. mover of this resolution (Mr. Irvine), or by other gentlemen of that group? Their minds are full of theories from people who have had no practical experience. As I said last year to the house, everything that is written has their respect; they worship type. Their hero is Gutenberg, the inventor of printing. I am sure that they must meet in the cellar of a printing house. They do not admit anything that is the subject of discussion. They believe only in type and in what is typeset, and they upset us with that, sometimes. They are not serious. They think they are serious but they are not. What they say is incredible, impracticable, unrealizable, and they know it. If they do not know it, I am sorry for them. It is always the same story with them. The state must take control of

Nationalization oj Banks
all the wealth of Canada because one day they hope to take power and use it for the great benefit of this country. That is their utopia-a utopian thought for them to think the people of this country will put them into power. But, Mr. Speaker, my electors are soundminded; the electors of any constituency are soundminded, and surely these hon. gentlemen to my left were not elected on speeches like the one we have just heard. No elector in this country would take seriously a man who speaks of such an important matter in such a childish way. He proves only one thing, that he does not at all realize the importance of the subject he is discussing, and I can only feel sorry for him.

subtopic: PROPOSAL THAT CREDIT AND CURRENCY SHALL BE CONTROLLED AND ADMINISTERED BY GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
The resolution before us reads:
That, in the opinion of this house, all banking facilities, including both the chartered banks and the central bank, should be nationalized as speedily as possible.
I told my hon. friend from Vegreville that he had great respect for books and typewritten matter and for that reason I bring to the house to-night a big book in which I find fifty-five questions which have been put to the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation in this house. These questions were put to them two years ago and have not yet been answered. One quotation from their sublime orations is this:
Major services and utilities and such productive and distributive enterprises as can be conducted most efficiently when owned in common (should be owned-and controlled) by public corporations responsible to the people's elected representatives.
On this, the following question was asked:
What would happen: (a) to the amounts of money deposited in chartered banks by private individuals; and (b) to life insurance held by them?
There are two motions relating to the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation and appearing on to-day's order paper-one already mentioned and another one in the name of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) in which he summarizes the program of his group. There is also one in the name of the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Kennedy) with regard to the Peace River railway.
It would be rather difficult for me to read the fifty-five questions already put to the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation group two years ago, but I have read one. There are many others however which I think should be read to the leader of that group when his resolution comes up. But let me tell my hon. friend in the faraway corner how I understand the learning of the banking business from the point of view of members of parliament. The first thing would be to read the old Bank Act and the amending act of last year and to compare the two. This is elementary; it is the basis of learning. They would learn much more about Canadian banking by reading the laws which they have helped to pass than by reading Sir Arthur Salter's great, theory of banking, or Schatt's theories, or the theories expounded by all the learned economists who know nothing about the laws which have been enacted in this country by all of us, including the hon. member who has not time to read the legislation which he himself has voted upon. It would also be very useful to my hon. friends

it would complete their education in this matter-to read the annual reports of the banks published in every daily newspaper as well as in the Canada Year Book, which was distributed free to us in years gone by. Another most interesting publication in regard to banking in this country is the Canada Gazette. I would suggest to my hon. friends that they also read the reports published by the Department of Finance showing the amount of money in the banks, in savings accounts, current accounts and so on. If my hon. friends can spare a moment from their scientific experiments in connection with foreign bankers, I commend to them very highly, first, the reading of our own bank acts and a comparison of them, then the annual reports of the banks, which are available to all and are published in the newspapers-if they asked the general managers of the banks for these reports I am sure they would receive them-then the official gazette, which comes from the king's printer. There are also reports each month under the signature of the Minister of Finance and they too are most interesting. If they will look at the last annual report tabled at the opening of this session by the Minister of Finance, they will find it very instructive. They should read all these reports going back to confederation and learn them by heart; I am sure they would enjoy reading them.
These various publications form the basis of banking knowledge, and though one may forget the exact figures one will remember in the main what has been said by these leading bankers. There is one thing which my hon. friends have discussed from a different
Nationalization oj Banks

angle, and that is reduction in the rate of interest. I did not listen to their speeches this afternoon because I know it is always the same story-they ask for a reduction in the rate of interest. A distinction should be drawn. There was a reduction of one-half of one per cent in the rate of interest the year before last, and last year another one-half of one per cent. Why? Was it at the request of the people at large in this country? Was it at the request of those who deposited tnoney in the banks? It was not the request of the depositors but at the request of the bankers themselves. They took advantage of what had been said by my hon. friends at the extreme left of the house, to come and tell the government that it was most important to have a reduction in the rate of interest on deposits in order to give an opportunity to the banks to make credit more available. If my hon. friends will look into the annual reports of the banks, the official gazette, and the monthly reports of the Minister of Finance, they will see that the amount of savings in the chartered banks at the present time is about the same as it was five years ago, with the exception that there is a little more inflated money in circulation now, at their request, than before. It is nearly the same amount of money, but the interest rate has been cut by one-third. What was the amount that was in the savings accounts in the chartered banks? It was 81,400,000,000. My hon. friends know that very well. One per cent on that amount is 814,000,000; the first cut of one-half of one per cent meant $7,000,000, and another similar cut followed. To cover their losses, the banks took advantage of what was said by my hon. friends to bring pressure to bear on the government- the Minister of Finance will not deny this because it is the fact-to allow them to pay less to the depositors. The result is that that amount, the difference in the rate of interest, has not been given to the customers of the banks, the depositors; it has been kept by the banks themselves to cover their losses. My hon. friends know very well; it is public knowledge, that when a bank lent $12,000,000 on a man's own signature some years ago, that man never paid back to the bank what he got from it. The reduction in the rate of interest has been enjoyed by the bank, and its customers, the depositors, have suffered an equal loss.
Is the government adopting the policy of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation- no profit? Does the government intend to curtail that very legitimate profit that comes from the rate of interest on deposits made

in the chartered banks? When I said that there was only this difference between the Prime Minister and the leader of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation, that the Prime Minister was clean-shaven and the other was not, I think I was right. I am not saying that as a joke; I say that seriously because they have arrived at the same conclusion. We hear the Prime Minister repeating all the time: Our banks are safe; they are solid; we have nothing to fear about the future of our banks. That is all right. It is why people invested their money in the banks. But if, owing to the reduction in the rate of interest, this brings people no legitimate profit, they will take their money out of the banks and put it into unsound investments to get supposedly easy money, to make easy profits, and then, as has happened in the past, they will lose their money.
A tremendous responsibility rests upon the shoulders of the Minister of Finance. He was in the chamber a minute ago; I am sorry he has left. By virtue of the old Bank Act he had all the power that is now given to the central bank to control banking in general in this country. He could make every bank tremble; he was boss of finance. I remember very well-and every member should remember this-that not long after the minister had been sworn in as minister of finance, someone from this side of the house asked him about a change, saying: What is the reason for that change? The minister's answer was: I have been advised so and so by the officials of my department. I did not say anything at the time but I was very sorry for the hon. gentleman, for whom I have a great regard, that he could not give a better answer to the house. What was his answer? It was: "I do not know; the officers of my department do that." Are we to live any more in such a state of bureaucracy? Is a minister of the crown to be led by third-rate clerks in his department? Every time a question of such importance as that is asked, we are answered with a smile. A smile is a nice thing, but from a minister of the crown it is no answer. I am sorry to say this because I have a high regard and respect for the hon. gentleman, but apparently he has not studied the whole matter so as to be able to give a satisfactory answer to members of parliament.
Let me go further. In a most interesting report published in December, I see that the general manager of one of the banks said: We are generous; we pay much more interest to the depositors than we pay to the shareholders. Is it possible that people can say

Nationalization of Banks
such a thing as that? That man should know; everyone knows that the number of shareholders is much less than that of depositors. On the other hand the rate of interest paid to the depositors is only two per cent while the rate paid to shareholders is twelve per cent. I do not put the blame only on the Minister of Finance; I put it on the whole government for letting men of outstanding character in this country make such silly statements in order to deceive the people. This will cause more prejudice against the bankers than even the losses sustained by the banks, because people will say: men like that are not serious.
Is it necessary to nationalize our banks? I do not believe so. I believe in the old order; I believe the act was well enough drafted to permit the Minister of Finance to have absolute control over the banks. He had the power to send in his inspectors to check the banking, to know what was going on, to check the collateral securities. Is it because the minister and the government were afraid to take such a step that they created that new organization which is called the central bank? I have been in the main at one with the policy of my party, but in my humble opinion the fact that the minister did not take the responsibility that he should with regard to banking is the reason why the central bank was necessary; it was necessary because the minister was saying in the house that he was acting in accordance with the views of the officers of his department and also because he did not and the government did not dare to take the responsibility of checking those sharks of finance that we have in Montreal and Toronto and of whom everyone knows. That was the point. Is it fair, because a man has got under false pretences a sum of $12,000,000 from the banks; is it fair because bankers lacked judgment in lending so much money to him, that all the depositors in the banks should have first one-half of one per cent and later one per cent less interest in order to cover the banks' losses and the shareholders receive twelve per cent while the depositors get only two per cent? Is that fair? Is it just? When the Prime Minister comes along afterwards and says: Our institutions are sound. He says, "Ready, aye, ready," when they come to him for such favours. The shareholders are the privileged few; they get the high rate of interest of twelve per cent, and in order that the banks might continue to pay that twelve per cent to the shareholders the government, after hearing what the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation group said in this house and outside, reduced the rate of interest paid to the farmers, paid to widows, paid to
men in industry, paid to anyone who has a dollar in the bank. First they reduced it by half of one per cent, and then to two per cent. The indictment should not be against the bankers; it should be against those who sit on the treasury benches and who have not the courage, have not the guts to stop the bankers from exploiting the people and doing things like that. The responsibility lies with them. When the Prime Minister says our system has a sound foundation, his very acts are the dynamite that blows up that foundation of confidence in our institutions. That is why I regret the step which has been taken by this government, which cannot be justified either before this house or before the electorate of this country. It is not for me to give names; everyone knows about it. The shareholders of the banks get a rate of interest of twelve per cent; the depositors get two per cent, and it may go down to one and a half per cent or to nothing -no profit, the Cooperative Commonwealth theory. The Cooperative Commonwealth Federation and the government will kiss each other and not be ashamed of themselves. They will be able to say: We are going to socialize now; the government have adopted socialist views, thus destroying the confidence of our people in our institutions, depriving the people of legitimate income and exposing them to the lure of unsound investments because they cannot get reasonable interest from the banks. This is the wonderful situation we have just a year after the last revision of the Bank Act.
Let me tell my hon. friends in the corner one thing. I am friendly with them; I have some very dear friends among them, and they know that. I have friends everywhere in the house. I see them now smiling.

I am glad to see my hon. friend the Minister of Finance returning to his seat now. I was about to conclude my speech; I have just a word to say to him. He knows I have regard for him, but what I was very sorry for was the reduction in the rate of interest paid by the banks to depositors. The minister knows that the depositors get only two per cent, while the shareholders get twelve per cent. The depositors had their rate of interest cut from three to two per cent, while the shareholders had twelve per cent. I said the bankers went to him in his own office to ask a reduction in the rate of interest, taking advantage of what was said by the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation, and thus the bankers saved $14,000,000 last year. I said that before the minister was here; I repeat it now he is back in his seat. Last year, in reply to a question put by an hon. member on this side as to why such a change was made, I repeat the following answer was given:	"It was recommended by
the officials of my department." Surely the minister was not serious in that. He should be the boss; he could make the banks tremble. He was the boss under the old legislation. Because a thing is recommended by a third-rate clerk is no reason why it should be acceptable in the national interest. Let him use his own judgment; it is much better than the opinion of his clerks. They may give him information and facts; that is all right, but he should draw his own conclusions, in order to be able to defend his policy in this house. This is most important. I do not say that in an offensive way, but it could not be repeated too often. May I tell him also that I regret very much that we have now a central bank,

for this reason; that before, under the old act, the minister had all power; he could send the inspectors of his department to every bank to check what was done. Will it be so easy for him to do that now? The central bank was first asked for by hon. members on the extreme left for the purpose of getting easy credit. But that proved to be impossible. It is now being looked upon not as a source of credit but only as a means of control, because the Minister of Finance did not take advantage of the control he had at his disposal.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is I think unnecessary, and certainly it is far from my intention, that I should discuss at any length the provisions and meaning of the resolution now before the house. Those provisions and that meaning have been discussed and amplified this afternoon by men more competent than I to discuss such matters. It might not be out of place, however, for me to suggest that if the principle upon which this resolution is based is accepted by the house or by any part of the house, then the resolution itself, in terms, becomes essentially logical, and its logic is inescapable.
The principle, as I see it, is that finance, using the word in its widest possible sense and with all its implications, should be considered rather as a public utility than as a private industry, that it should be operated and controlled by the state for the use and the good of all the people within the state rather than operated and controlled by individuals or groups of individuals for theii private profit. If this principle is accepted then I think it must follow as an inescapable conclusion, Mr. Speaker, that in order to put this principle into effect the instruments through which the principle is applied and the medium through which finance is controlled and distributed also should be under the complete ownership and control of the people of this country. I think no one in this house would suggest that in the case of the water supply, say, of some great municipality such as Ottawa, the water itself should be considered a public utility and that it should be the duty of the municipality to furnish that water in ample quantity and of clear and excellent quality to all the citizens, yet that the municipality should permit the machinery and the pipes conveying that water to the citizens to be owned and controlled by private individuals for their private profit. To my mind the cases, while not wholly similar, certainly are somewhat analogous. And that

principle, Mr. Speaker, which for many years has been urged from this corner of the house, which has come to be looked upon with favour by a large percentage of the people of Canada and which has been finally accepted by the Liberal party, I believe is a principle which should be endorsed by this house and, if endorsed, should be carried into effect by the acceptance and carrying out of this resolution.
I did not rise, however, so much to discuss the resolution itself as to make some comment on what has been said by others. In this I am in somewhat the same position as others who have spoken, many of whom have stated that they had not intended to speak but that some remarks made by other members had forced them to their feet. I find myself somewhat in that position; it was largely because of certain remarks made by the hon. member for West Edmonton (Mr. Stewart) that I rose to-night. When the hon. member spoke I noted that he was inclined to be, I shall not say indignant but surprised, grieved and a little disappointed at the vote cast by the majority of the members in this comer of the house last session in respect of the central bank bill. I was not surprised at the hon. gentleman's attitude. In the first place he has not had the advantage we in this corner have had, of sitting as a minority group in this house during nine years of Liberal and four years of Conservative rule; he has not been taught by long and bitter experience the great necessity of toleration and some degree of willingness to accept half a loaf rather than have no bread. During all these years we have learned that such is the case; we would have made no progress and nothing would have been accomplished had we not been ready to go step by step, taking each time the step which might be taken, hoping it would lead to better things, insisting only that the step should be such as would truly lead onward rather than backward. Again I was not surprised because history will show, and experience has taught, that there is no zealot so intolerant and uncompromising in his zeal as the recent convert. We have all met with and experienced this situation, that the man who rushes forward, offering you no alternative save the koran or the sword, that you must believe with him or perish, is the man who only recently has seen the light. Under such circumstances it is usual for those zealous for the truth to insist that no compromise is possible, that no jot or title of the truth, the whole truth, must be pared away, but that we must accept every single beauty in that Mohammedan
paradise if we are to go to paradise at all; that no diminution in that harem must be permitted but that the entity, in all its perfection, must be accepted or rejected as the case may be.
That has not been our course, Mr. Speaker; as I have suggested before, had that been our course such progress as has been made in the past would have been impossible. Last year when we reached the time for the final vote to be taken on the third reading of the central bank bill; when all amendments had to be discarded and all alternatives left aside; when we came to the point that we must vote for a central bank, privately owned indeed but largely publicly controlled, or vote against it and in favour of retaining the system exactly as it was before, we believed our course was clear. Generally speaking, we would not take the course which I suggested was consciously or unconsciously the course of those who opposed that legislation, of aligning ourselves consciously or unconsciously with every force and every interest in this country that has continuously opposed the idea of any state control, any centralized authority, or any central bank of any kind. We believe this is a step forward, as we believe that legislation was a step forward. We believed not only that the immediate situation would be improved but that, in that improvement, we would have created the machinery, wTith centralized control and authority, which at any time at the will of this parliament might be converted into an entirely publicly owned institution. I can only say that the people whom I represent are at least as ardent in their support of public ownership of the central bank as are those supporting any hon. gentleman to my right. In spite of their weakness in sending me here as their member they are not unintelligent. They fully understood both the purpose and the sanity of our vote, and the purpose at least of those who have criticized us so severely.
Having said that, Mr. Speaker, I have fulfilled the purpose for which I rose. I desire first to associate myself with those who consistently, in season and out and before the idea itself became popularized, have held that finance in its essence, in its utilization, is a state function, a public utility, and that in order to utilize it to the full in that capacity the instruments and the conduits by which it is administered and through which it flows also must be public institutions. I wished only to make some comment on the criticism which has been offered, and having

subtopic: FACILITIES FOR REFRIGERATION AND DISTRIBUTION OF BAIT
FACILITIES FOR REFRIGERATION AND DISTRIBUTION OF BAIT
speechtext:
Whereas the deep-sea fishermen of the Atlantic coast, and especially those in the Northumberland straits, the baie de Chaleur and gulf of St. Lawrence, are seriously hampered in their work by lack of means of obtaining an adequate and seasonal supply of bait, especially for the cod fishing branch of the industry;
And whereas it is beyond the means of private initiative to provide the necessary facilities for the procuring and distribution of such bait, as well as its conservation;
And whereas the establishment of such facilities at central points would greatly enhance the importance of the fishing industry by an increased catch;
And whereas such increase in the industry would provide work for a very large number of fishermen who are now idle because of the difficulty in securing bait;
Therefore be it resolved, that, in the opinion of this house, it is expedient that the government should take into immediate consideration the establishment at important centres of a number of refrigerator plants of such dimensions as the Department of Fisheries may consider adequate to meet the needs of the industry, and at the same time give consideration to the best method of distribution of the bait required.
He said: Mr. Speaker, we have heard in the last few days a great deal of discussion touching the hardships that the farmers of our country have been called upon to undergo during the last four or five years in this period of world wide depression. May I be permitted, sir, to-night to say to the house that the farmers of Canada are not the only ones who have suffered in their industry during this period of depression. The fishing industry of the Dominion of Canada is a very important one; I think we occupy the third position in the world in regard to the deep sea fisheries.
The fishermen of the province of New Brunswick-I speak for that province because I am better acquainted with its fishing industry and the needs of its fishermen-have suffered from various sources during the last four or five years. True it was not the depression that brought about the losses by storms and other losses that were suffered at sea by our fishermen, but these only added to the hardships that they had to undergo during the period of the depression.

The low prices which our fishermen have been forced to accept for the products of the sea during the last four or five years have been such that unless they are aided in some way to overcome their overhead expenses, thereby lessening the cost of production, they will have to go out of business.
Last week we had a bill before the house providing for a lower rate of interest on loans to farmers, a movement which I am pleased to be able to say I supported. It was pointed out then that a lower rate of interest would aid the farmers by reducing their overhead expenses and thus in some degree compensate them for the low prices they are receiving for their products. It was also pointed out that the products of the farm had been reduced in price to a greater extent than the products of any other industry. I beg to differ from that statement, Mr. Speaker. It is true that the prices of farm products have gone down very considerably, but they have not gone down in comparison with the very low prices which are being received by the fishermen for the products of the sea. To-day the product of the sea is sold at prices that really place the fisherman in this position, that he has to choose between starvation and giving up the industry and seeking employment in some other line. That condition, in my opinion, can be remedied; and since the government is paternal enough to assist other industries I feel it my duty to invoke their aid in behalf of the fishermen.
In this resolution I suggest the establishment of refrigerating plants to provide means whereby the fishermen may obtain bait by a process easier than that through which they now get that necessity. So far as the fishermen in my county are concerned, we have a fleet of between two and three hundred vessels engaged in fishing. They leave their homes on Monday, remaining on the banks of Northumberland straits and other places throughout the week and returning on Saturday or sometimes Sunday morning. They have no time to get bait between their arrival and their departure on the next fishing trip.
In the past, in Gloucester county, we were able to obtain the clam in very large quantities as bait for cod fishing, but to-day the clam is becoming scarce. It costs a great deal more to procure clam bait than it did in the past. One reason is its scarcity, and another is the establishment of clam canning factories in the county. In Gloucester to-day there is the largest clam factory in the world, and the price is such that it no longer pays the fisherman, as it did in the past, to buy

Deep Sea Fisheries
clam for bait. Indeed, he has not the means to do so even if he wanted to buy clams, with prices as they are now.
The question may be interjected-why was this movement not made sooner? Why was it not made seven or eight years ago? Well, up to the time this depression struck the industry, prices for fish, especially for cod, were very reasonable and our fishermen could then afford, at the prices received six, seven or eight years ago, for dry salted and semipickled cod, to purchase the bait necessary to carry on their industry. To-day, at the reduced price which they receive for their fish, which is almost $2.50 or $3 per quintal less than it was seven years ago, they cannot afford it. They require some assistance, and I was going to suggest the establishment of small refrigerating plants in several central districts of northern New Brunswick or any other part of the Atlantic coast. I am speaking especially for the fishermen of northern New Brunswick, but in this regard I do not wish to be understood as being sectional in my views.
I suggest the establishment of small refrigerating plants under the absolute control and management of the government. Why do I put emphasis on that point? I do so because refrigerating plants under the cooperative system, owned in part by the government and in part by the fishermen as shareholders in the company, have not been a success. Too many jealousies arose. There was too much favouritism and the consequence was that these plants disappeared. Under previous arrangements, under the cooperative system as between the government and the fishing industry, the government paid so much per cent and the fishermen subscribed so much, and after a period of years the government's share in the undertaking would disappear and the fishermen could buy out the whole business. The result was that certain large fish dealers got into their heads the notion that they would buy out these plants, and in order to do so they bought up shares held by individual fishermen. In consequence, these large shippers of fish became the sole proprietors of the refrigerating plants and the fishermen no longer derived from the undertaking that benefit which it had been intended they should obtain.
Another reason why these plants failed in the past was that we were under the old system of ice freezing. We used ice houses. Ice was cut in the winter and hauled into these buildings and used for freezing during the summer. Improvements have been made
since that time, and under the new system now in practice in certain parts of Canada there is no need to resort to the ice freezing process at all.
Now this is not an experiment that I am going to propose; it has been tried and found successful. The government of Quebec, owning and administering their own fisheries, have inaugurated the system of establishing small refrigerating plants. On the bay of Chaleur is to be found, on the north side, the coast line of the province of Quebec, and on the south side we have the coast line of New Brunswick; and here we find on the north side the fishermen being provided with the means of conservation for their bait, while on the south side no means whatever are provided for the fishermen of the counties of Gloucester, Restigouche, Northumberland and Kent.
I have been looking carefully into this matter and have obtained plans and specifications. I have received, not estimates but actual prices of these refrigerators which have already been established, some in Prince Edward Island, I believe, and others in the province of Quebec. I find that a freezer that will freeze one ton of bait per day, and having a storage capacity of from fifteen to twenty tons, will cost, actual cost, $4,600 fully equipped. One that will freeze two tons per day, with storage capacity of from twenty-five to thirty-five tons, will cost $6,000, and one that will freeze three tons, with a storage capacity of from fifty to eighty tons will cost $10,000.
I do not intend to recommend the $10,000 process; I believe that the second process, freezing two tons, with a storage capacity of from twenty-five to thirty-five tons, and at a cost of $6,000, will meet all the requirements, at least so far as I know, in the county I have the honour to represent. And on this point there is something I would direct to the attention of the government. I would ask them to investigate the matter and to have the officers of their department go over the whole situation. Have them visit the various districts or have representatives of the fishing industry from those various districts meet them at some point where they can discuss the matter fully, take into serious consideration and report to the government.
I think I have explained this matter so that it will be readily understood by everyone; it is not necessary for me to take up any further time of the house. I hope the resolution will meet with the approval of all hon. members. I am not asking for the expenditure of public money; I am asking
Deep Sea Fisheries

that the matter be looked into, and if it is found feasible, then the government in its wisdom may decide upon the amount of money it will expend in aiding the fishermen.

speechtext:
I want to add a few words on the subject of the speech just delivered by the hon. member for Gloucester (Mr. Veniot). We have in Quebec a very important fishing industry, notably in the counties of Gaspe, Bonaventure, Matane, and on the north shore of the St. Lawrence. The government of Quebec has established there several refrigerating plants for bait. It is true that the administration of fisheries belongs to the federal government, out I do not see why we should not have cooperation between the two governments. This matter was discussed at length last year and two years ago, and I think the fishermen of Quebec, being taxpayers, should benefit to the same extent as the rest of Canada in respect of the facilities afforded to them. The refrigerating plants built in Quebec are not well equipped to meet the situation. The government should establish in those counties in that province refrigerating plants such as have been asked for by the hon. member for Gloucester, and I should think in most of those places small plants would meet the requirements. An expenditure of from $6,000 to $10,000 would build refrigerating plants that would meet the situation, and the fishermen would benefit a great deal. From July 1 to September 1, I have seen fishermen all along the coast of the lower St. Lawrence idle because they cannot get bait. If refrigerating plants were established so that they could get their bait requirements, those fishermen would not be idle but would work all summer long and would not be on the dole as they are at present.
In the Magdalen islands, which is part of my constituency, the fishing industry is under the control of the federal government. There the government of Quebec, although they have nothing to do with the fisheries of that part, aid the fishermen by giving them boats and money to help the industry. I do not see why the federal government should not do the same thing for the rest of the province of Quebec. Therefore I strongly favour the resolution moved by the hon. member for Gloucester and I hope the government will take steps immediately to investigate the matter and give it proper attention.

subtopic: FACILITIES FOR REFRIGERATION AND DISTRIBUTION OF BAIT
speechtext:
May I be permitted to make a few observations with regard to the resolution of my hon. friend the ex-Postmaster General (Mr. Veniot). We have on the east coast of New
(Mr. Veniot.]
Brunswick what is admittedly the best dry salt cod fishing in the maritime provinces. Along with lobster, salmon, smelts and oyster fishing, this industry serves to employ a large proportion of our people, and on the north Shore of New Brunswick, particularly what is known as the Miramichi district, in numbers employed fishing is second only to our great basic industry.
With the terms of the resolution as drafted one must be in reasonable accord, but it is to be regretted that those engaged in the fishing industry have not seen fit to take advantage not only of the regulations already existing in respect to the matter of bait but particularly of the legislation adopted at the last session of parliament when the Natural Products Marketing Act was placed upon the statute books. Unfortunately the fishing industry on the east coast of New Brunswick, as is well known to the hon. member for Gloucester, is really as to ownership and marketing facilities concentrated in the hands of a few large firms, who, I may say with great respect and deference, are not doing justice to the fishermen so far as the price for their catch is concerned. Take for instance the price paid for smelts to-day-and in this connection I may say with some considerable satisfaction that the Miramichi is the greatest smelt fishing river in the world. The price to the fishermen is only five cents per pound on the ice, while in the towns, the local domestic market, the price exacted is fifteen cents per pound, and smelts, as is well known, demand a high price on the Boston and New York markets. Therefore I say in all sincerity, and I am sure hon. members will agree with me, that those engaged in this industry should take advantage of the provisions of the marketing act. In this connection a campaign of education is essential. Members from Nova Scotia will appreciate the importance of the work accomplished in 1929 by Doctor Coady in his capacity as organizer in forming various cooperative societies in that province. Unfortunately the work of organization in New Brunswick did not commence until the winter of 1929, and due to transportation facilities being unfavourable at that time Doctor Coady was forced to abandon the work, which has not since been prosecuted.
May I commend to the acting Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Stirling) the advisability of studying, if he will, the question of organizing cooperative societies among the fishermen along the east coast of New Brunswick, and

Deep Sea Fisheries
particularly of the county of Northumberland. I notice in the estimates a vote of $4,050 to the United Maritime Fishermen's Association, subject as to expenditure to provisions to be enacted by the governor in council. May I suggest that a fair and equitable proportion of this vote might be well expended in the promotion of a campaign to organize cooperative societies on the north shore of New Brunswick. In this connection, if his services are easily obtainable, as I believe they will be, I know of no more outstanding and eminent authority than Doctor Coady, who did such excellent work along that line in Nova Scotia in 1929. At the same time I should like to pay tribute to Mr. Mclnerney, a former north shore boy, who is now acting secretary of the United Maritime Fishermen's Association. I should like also to congratulate the minister upon the good work achieved by the officials of his department, notably Colonel A. L. Barry, who is the supervisor on the north shore. However, I believe that a great deal of the difficulty our fishermen are experiencing could be solved by cooperative marketing. I am confident that if a campaign of education along this line were undertaken, excellent results would follow. It would at the same time furnish the opportunity of educating the people as to the necessity of respecting the existing regulations, because between illegal fishing and the lack of cooperative marketing the great fishing industry is suffering severely.
I do not know that I favour the idea of the department establishing a number of refrigerator plants, I believe that if private enterprise were properly directed-I mean the larger fishing concerns-they would make the necessary expansion. But as to the condition of those engaged in cod fishing, I concur in the remarks of the hon. member for Gloucester. I would respectfully urge upon the department the necessity of instituting some campaign along the lines indicated, and particularly of adding a rider that part of the proposed vote of $1,050 for the United Maritime Fishermen's Association be applied towards the expense of the organization of cooperative societies on the north shore of New Brunswick.

speechtext:
As a seconder of this motion perhaps I need not say I am very much in accord with the sentiments thereof. The matter of bait for fishermen is very important. The fisheries of this country depend to a great extent upon whether or not the fishermen are able to obtain bait or not. Perhaps I had

My hon. friend is not very consistent. In discussing the bait freezer question he said that instead of the government building these bait freezers and providing bait for the fishermen this might well be done by private enterprise. If in the opinion of my hon. friend it is better for private enterprise to build bait freezers and provide bait for the fishermen why cannot the same private enterprise handle the product of the fishermen and put it on the market, whether in fresh or salt condition? So my hon. friend is not very consistent.
However, as I have said this is a very important question. It is one in which I have been interested for the last forty years. I agree with the hon. member for Gloucester that there is great need for some arrangement by which the fishermen of the Atlantic coast, Northumberland straits, baie des Chaleurs and gulf of St. Lawrence should have means of obtaining an adequate and seasonable supply of bait not only for cod fishing but also for their other kinds of fishing. We live in an age in which large amounts of money are being expended by governments, federal and provincial. The hon. member for Gaspe (Mr. Brasset) told us that the Quebec government was spending money to establish bait freezers. This government is also spending large sums in different ways. For instance a day or two ago the Minister of Finance (Mr. Rhodes) moved a resolution to amend the Canadian Farm Loan Act. We were told that a sum of $90,000,000 was to be provided. I have no objection if that sum is necessary in the interests of the farmers, but it seems to me that if this government and the taxpayers of this country are going to raise $90,000,000 to lend to farmers the government should also take into consideration the necessities of the fisheries industry, for which a comparatively small amount of money would do a great deal.
In that regard I am reminded of a statement made by the Prime Minister in the election of 1930. No doubt he was in earnest and sincere; no doubt he had the best interests of the country at heart when he made certain statements at meetings in different parts of this country. He said in the city of Halifax that "he would throw the whole financial power of the state behind the fishing industry." That was a very wide statement for a gentleman to make who desired to be returned to power as prime minister of this country. But what has the Prime Minister done in the last four years, what has his government done in the last four years to "throw any financial power of the state behind that great industry?" That industry has far greater possibilities than
(Mr. DuB.I
any other natural industry in this country; the surface has been hardly scratched, and it does not cost the people of this country a cent. If you take the mines, once the ore is taken out nothing is left but holes in the ground. When you take off the wheat, potatoes or other crops from the farms you have to cultivate and fertilize before you can grow anything more. If you go to the forests and cut down trees it takes twenty or thirty years to produce a new crop. There is no doubt that the fisheries of this country offer greater opportunity to put more men at work than any other industry in Canada, yet this government has done nothing to aid that industry.
I do not blame this government altogether. I have been in this parliament for eighteen years, and during that time the fisheries of Canada have been the rag-tag and bob-tail of practically every department of the government. I do not object to my hon. friend from Yale (Mr. Stirling) being the acting Minister of Fisheries; as my hon. friend from Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot) would say, he is a personal friend of mine, and in anything I say I hope the minister will not think I am referring to him personally. But even before I came here the fisheries of this country were not getting a square deal, and they have not had a show since then. The fisheries department has been tied up to some other department. First it was tied up to the militia department, from 1917 to 1921 or 1922. Then it was put in with the marine department, until a number of hon. members on both sides of the house, including my hon. friend from Digby-Annapolis (Mr. Short), succeeded in showing the importance of'this great industry. After a number of years we got the government to see that the two departments should be separated, which was done in 1930. We know what happened then, and we know what has happened since. When the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) was returned to office he appointed a minister of fisheries, but within two years in his wisdom he again amalgamated the departments of marine and fisheries. Today there is no minister of fisheries, and the department has gone back to the Department of National Defence. So I say, Mr. Speaker, that my right hon. friend is not carrying out the pledge he made to the people of Halifax in 1930, when he said "he would throw the whole financial power of the state behind the fisheries industry."
With regard to the matter of bait for the fishermen, away back in 1906, when Mr. Fielding was the minister from Nova Scotia, the Liberal government voted some money for the purpose of establishing what were known

Deep Sea Fisheries
as ice and salt bait freezers. A number of these freezers were erected in Nova Scotia and New Brunswick, the government paying fifty per cent of the cost and the fishermen raising the other fifty per cent through cooperative efforts. I regret to say, however, that after one or two years jealousies and other difficulties arose with the result that these freezers were not a success. Another reason for their failure was the fact that in those days fresh bait was much more plentiful than it is to-day, and as everyone knows who is interested at all in the fishing industry, fishermen will not take frozen or salt bait when they can secure fresh bait. As a result, although the government of the day was sincere in its efforts to supply proper bait facilities, these bait freezers were not a success.
Later the government arranged, through the Department of Agriculture, to grant one-third of the cost of what were known as ammonia freezers. Several of these freezers were established at different points in the maritime provinces, on a large scale. It was found impossible, however, when these freezers were established at central points, for the fishermen in the outports and the villages along the shores to Obtain bait from those central freezers. So, while these freezers did a great deal of good and a number of fishermen were able to obtain bait from them, it was found that the scheme did not entirely fill the bill. In 1927, if I remember correctly, after Of became the representative of the constituency of Antigonish-Guysborough-the best constituency in Canada, I might say-I realized that the people in my district were far removed from both the bait freezers and the market. I endeavoured to impress upon the government the necessity of arranging not only for a bait supply but also for a method of marketing the fish. Steamers were therefore chartered by the government to convey bait to the fishermen and also to take away their catch to central points.
Since this government came into power a steamer, which was arranged for in 1928, still goes around Chedabucto bay carrying bait for the fishermen of Canso and vicinity, and also for the fishermen of Richmond county, but that is not sufficient. It is true that for a number of years there was a large bait freezer in the town of Canso, but the company ceased operations, with the result that the fishermen of Canso, Whitehead, Port Felix, Fox island, Queensport and other places are not able to obtain bait at certain seasons of the year. Their only chance at present is to secure bait from this small boat 92582-31
which is put on by the government in the summer season, or to secure the bait direct from the traps when the herring strike. Following the closing of this bait freezer the result has been, so far as Canso is concerned, that what was once a great industry is now practically wiped out. Hundreds of men in Canso to-day are either on relief or barely able to make a mean living due to the fact that there are no bait facilities available which would permit them to fish whenever they were willing to go out on the Atlantic ocean to the fishing grounds. So I say this resolution is very important, and a large freezer and cold storage plant should be erected at Canso.
Several years ago the government decided that a large bait freezer and cold storage plant should be erected in Halifax. I believe that was in 1927, and if I remember correctly some 8670,000 was granted to a company which built the plant at a cost of some 82,500,000. That plant ran for several years, but to my surprise it was taken over by the harbour commission last year for something like 82,000,000. I do not think that was a good business deal. The harbour commission might have waited and made better terms, because the private corporation was anxious to sell. Instead of paying
82,000,000 for the plant, I believe it could have been bought for a great deal less. Certainly if the government, whether this government or the preceding government, could spend first 8670,000 and then an additional $2,000,000 for a cold storage and bait freezing plant in Halifax, they could arrange in view of all the circumstances to spend money to encourage the fisheries and effect improvements along the coasts of Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island, so that the fishermen in the different villages may have the facilities to procure bait for the purpose of catching fish in the summer season.
Not only did the government take over the plant at Halifax but I notice in Bill 138 of last session an amount of 8286,000 was voted for the construction of bulkhead and pier, 195 feet and 200 feet respectively, to provide site for two fish processing plants adjacent to the cold storage plant. Then there was another $354,000 voted for the construction of buildings for fish processing plants adjacent to the cold storage plant. Instead of spending about $600,000, in the city of Halifax I should think that amount could have been used to better advantage out where the people catch fish, and could have been given to help the people who need bait. One more thing I wish to say. The hon. member for Antigonish-Guysborough made some observations about the selling of fish. The hon. member for Northumberland (Mr. Mc-Dade) said something for which the hon. member for Antigonish-Guysborough took him to task. Well, that is part of the game. While I am not a smelt fisherman, yet I live right by a river where smelts are caught in great quantities, and I have often talked with the fishermen. It is true, as the hon. member for Antigonish-Guysborough said, that they sell this fish very readily themselves. I have seen our men pack the finest smelts in nice clean white boxes, iced, everything done as well as it could be done, and then ship them on consignment to the Boston market and often get good returns. But many times they get back scarcely enough to pay the expenses, and I have seen a bill come back for the express and duty and consignment charges. That has happened time and again. It seems to me a great pity that such an industry, carried on
fMr. Myers.]
by the best and hardiest of our race, could not by some cooperative means, whether under the marketing act or by cooperation among themselves, be organized so that they might secure a price in keeping with such arduous toil. I have seen in my own riding the finest codfish that ever came out of the water selling at the boatside or on the stage for three-quarters of a cent a pound, yet I have seen that same fish selling at the markets right in our own province at eight or nine cents a pound. It does not seem fair that the men who bear the burden and the heat of the day iand toil in the chilly night should have to sell their fish at such a starvation price.
Then around the shores of my province we need, besides bait freezers, accommodation for the protection of our boats. The north shore of Prince Edward Island faces right out into the gulf of St. Lawrence, and a north wind there kicks up a terrible sea. In some places we have harbours, in others there are none. In many places the fishermen have to haul their boats out at every tide and launch them again when they get out to sea. It seems to me that the Department of Public Works, if they want to spend a little money, could very well spend it around the shores of Prince Edward Island, and I presume-I am more charitable than my hon. friends on the other side of the house-around the shores of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick as well, to see to it that the fishermen of the maritime provinces are accommodated as well as the finances of the country will permit with breakwaters and wharves at which they can land their boats.
I have just one other thought in mind. We are doing a great deal for the labouring men and for the farmers, but I think I am correct when I say that the unemployment insurance bill does not provide for fishermen. Mr. Speaker, I wish to say a few
words on this resolution. I am somewhat in the position of the hon. member who just resumed his seat (Mr. Myers); I am neither a farmer nor a fisherman, but I happen to represent an agricultural and fishing district in the county of Charlevoix-Saguenay, on the north shore of the St. Lawrence. I am proud to support this resolution; I think it should receive the serious consideration of the government. I was rather surprised to hear the remarks of the hon. member for North Winnipeg (Mr. Heaps) a few moments ago; he did not seem to attach much importance to this resolution and
seemed to make light of the hon. member who moved it. I think, however, that may be due to the fact that he lives very far inland and may not be familiar with conditions in the fishing industry.
All the recommendations contained in the latter part of the resolution are being carried out in the good old province of Quebec. The government of that province have come to the assistance of the fishermen in providing refrigerating plants at various places along the north shore of the St. Lawrence. As I was visiting my constituents last summer, at a place called Havre St. Pierre they were erecting a refrigerating plant with the money of the provincial government, with nothing contributed by the federal government. At another place called Thunder River a refrigerating plant was built a few years ago by the provincial government in order to aid the fishermen of that district.

I heartily approve of this resolution, and I hope the government will give it very serious consideration.
